shortDescription: Czech consumer prices grew by 0.3% in August from July, driven by energy prices and services, while retail sales continued a solid expansion in July, data showed on Friday.

children: Czech consumer prices grew by 0.3% in August from July, driven by energy prices and services, while retail sales continued a solid expansion in July, data showed on Friday.

Markets are watching new data for clues on whether the central bank will follow up on its rate hike in June, the first in four years, as price growth is expected to climb above 3% in early 2027, partially due to base effects of an energy price subsidy introduced this year.
August price growth put year-on-year inflation at 1.9%, in line with market and central bank expectations.
Retail sales growth reached 4.8% in July, above a forecast in a Reuters poll of 4.5%, confirming strong consumer sentiment.

High energy prices and other impacts of the U.S. war on Iran have raised concern over inflation, as well as solid domestic growth and consumption, and government plans to widen the budget deficit next year.
On the year, services prices remained an inflation driver, with 4.5% growth.

Energy prices rose by 2.3% on the year but also by 2.2% on the month in August, the Czech Statistical Office said, while food prices continued to pull in the lower direction, with a 1.1% monthly drop.

"We still expect interest rate stability at the Czech National Bank's September meeting. However we believe that serious debate about an increase will return this year," UniCredit Chief Economist in Prague Martin Komrska said in a note.

"The development in global energy markets is not giving much optimism, core inflation remains elevated and a fresh domestic inflation risk is the outlook for government spending in the coming years," Komrska added.

While recent data and global developments have pointed to higher inflation, the outlook was somewhat dampened on Thursday by second-quarter wage growth and a large downward revision to the average wage increase reported for the first quarter.
